events.title: Whalebait Markets on Manifold
events.description: A "whalebait market" is the most degenerate form of gambling known to mankind. When a prediction market tries to predict _its own price_, the market degenerates into a winner-take-all contest to see who can put down the most money. Michael Wheatley will recount the history and strategy of this (thankfully dead) artform on Manifold.

events.title: Prediction markets = bounded rationality?!?
events.description:
Here's a style of question which has long intrigued AI scientists: What's the best way to make decisions when your brain is too tiny to run the best algorithm to make decisions? Similarly: given that you know the definition of pi, is it rational to take a 60-40 bet that the 180,023rd digit is odd (assuming the person offering you the bet hasn't computed it yet, but also knows the definition of pi)?

In this talk, I'll talk about two papers that try to get a grip on the problem of bounded rationality: "Logical Induction", by Garrabrant et al, and "A Theory of Bounded Inductive Rationality" by Oesterheld et al. I'll explain what these papers are trying to do, how they compare to other attempts to do the same thing, and how the use of prediction markets is key to each paper.

events.title: Finding truth without instant liquidity
events.description:
I'll attempt to define "truth" (as an ex-physicist) and recap how liquid PMs incentivize sharing it.
A problem is that liquidity is at risk and thus low in fair, diverse, sustainable real-money markets.
However, I'll argue that this does not mean that volume must be low when users are empowered to be market makers,

events.title: Lightning Talk: Prediction-Action Markets for Coordination
events.description: Non-risk-neutral agents can use prediction markets to hedge against undesired outcomes. If the aggregate preferences result in the market cap exceeding the cost of intervention, the prediction market becomes an action market incentivizing the aggregate desired world. This dynamic can be used as a coordination mechanism, assuming market bids always resolve, but this turns out to work less well for risk-averse agents than for risk-seeking agents. Such dynamics can be concretely probed with toy examples such as the prisoner's dilemma, exposing the assumptions that underpin "libertarian utopias".
